abstract: RNA polymerase II’s (RNAPII) C-terminal domain (CTD) contains five phosphorylation sites (pY1, pS2, pT4, pS5, and pS7). However, their regulatome and immediate functions remain elusive. Using the FeaSion (Feature-Screening-Function) strategy, we mapped RNAPII phosphorylation site-specific interactors and genomic occupancy, revealing links to preferential gene length, exon number, and transcription factor binding. CRISPR-FACS screens identified different candidate regulators modulating individual phosphorylation sites. Rapid replacement showed site-specific mutations influence different transcriptional processes, histone modifications (H3K36me3 and H2A.Zac), and preferentially affect developmental and signaling genes. Moreover, we demonstrate kinases CLK1/4 and YES1 directly regulate RNAPII transcription—via site-specific CTD phosphorylation—to control developmental, metabolic, and signal transduction programs. Our findings reveal an expanded regulatory network involving >100 kinase and phosphatases that potentially orchestrate CTD phosphorylation beyond their canonical functions, establishing a multilayered phospho-regulatory network with broad implications for gene expression control in development and disease.

MATERIALS AND METHODS
Cell lines and cell culture

A549 cells were cultured in high-glucose Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM) (500 ml; Sigma-Aldrich #D5796) supplemented with 10% (v/v) fetal bovine serum (VivaCell, #C04001-500) and 1% (v/v) penicillin-streptomycin (Gibco, #15140-122). To replace WT RNAPII with RNAPII WT, Y1F, S2A, T4V, S5A, or S7A mutants, cells were pretreated with Dox (2 μg/ml; Sigma-Aldrich, #D9891) for 24 hours, and then dTAGV-1 (MedChemExpress, #HY-145514) was added to the culture medium with final concentration of 100 nM for indicated time. Plasmids and cell lines construction
To construct RPB1

Then, we used CRISPR-Cas9 to knockout the endogenous RPB1 by transfecting RPB1-specific sgRNA into these cells, which is annealed into the Cas9-mCherry–expressing PX330 backbone (Addgene, #42230). After 2 days, GFP and mCherry double-positive cells were selected with FACS, and monoclonal cells were collected and identified with western blotting. For RNAPII mutant constructs, we fused HA and HaloTag with RPB1 CDS containing either WT or RPB1 phosphorylation mutants (Y1F, S2A, T4V, S5A, and S7A) and cloned them into the tet-on promoter-based PiggyBac vector. We cotransfected the PiggyBac vector with the pBase vector into the RPB1

For KO plasmid construction, we annealed sgRNA oligos into lentiGuide-Puro backbone (Addgene, #52963) and subjected to lentivirus production (sgRNAs, see table S7). Then, the A549 Cas9 cells were infected with individual lentiviruses and selected with puromycin (2 μg/ml) for 2 days.
Lentivirus production and infection
HEK293T cells were plated 24 hours before lentivirus packaging. Lentivirus was generated by cotransfecting the sgRNA plasmids, along with pMD2.G (Addgene, #12259) and psPAX2 (Addgene, #12260) into HEK293T cells using polyethylenimine (PEI). After 12 hours, the medium was replaced with fresh culture medium containing 1% bovine serum albumin (BSA), 1 mM sodium pyruvate, and 1 mM sodium butyrate, and the lentiviruses were harvested 48 hours after transfection. For infection, lentiviruses were added to the culture medium along with polybrene (8 μg/ml; Beyotime, #C0351). After 24 hours, the infected cells were subjected to puromycin selection.

Afterward, the membrane was incubated for 1 hour at room temperature with the appropriate secondary antibody conjugated to horseradish peroxidase. The protein bands were visualized using chemiluminescence, and the images were processed with Adobe Photoshop (v.26.2.0).
Cell cycle analysis
The WT RNAPII was replaced with RNAPII mutants by treating cells with Dox (2 μg/ml) for 24 hours and 100 nM dTAGV-1 for 12 hours. After replacement, Hoechst 33342 (5 μg/ml; Beyotime, #C1022) and 200 nM Janelia Fluor 549 HaloTag ligand were added to the culture medium and incubated for 30 min. After staining, cell samples were collected and subjected to FACS analysis. Janelia Fluor 549–positive cells were gated, and cell cycle phases were identified with Hoechst 33342 contents. Cell number in different cell cycle phases were analyzed with FlowJo (v10.8.1). Cell numbers in each phase were normalized to total cell number, and stacked bar chart was plotted with custom R script.
Cell proliferation assay
Cells were seeded into a 96-well plate and treated with Dox (2 μg/ml) for 48 hours to induce the expression of RNAPII mutants. After 2 days, 100 nM dTAGV-1 was added to the culture medium to degrade WT RPB1, which would be replaced with RNAPII mutants. Cell proliferation was assessed at each time point using the M5 Hiper Cell Counting Kit 8 (Mei5, #MF128-01), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Specifically, at each time point, the kit reagents were added to the cells, and after a 2 hours of incubation, absorbance at 490 nm was measured using a multimode plate reader (PerkinElmer, VICTORX3). Wells without cells served as blank controls. Data were analyzed using two-sided
t

Fluorescence imaging
The WT RNAPII was replaced with RNAPII mutants by treating cells with Dox (2 μg/ml) for 24 hours and 100 nM dTAGV-1 for 4 hours. Cells were seeded on glass coverslips and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde at room temperature for 15 min. Permeabilization was performed with 0.2% Triton X-100 in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for 15 min, followed by blocking with 4% BSA in PBS for 40 min. Cells were then incubated overnight at 4°C with the RNPII antibody (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, #sc-55492), MED1 antibody (Abcam, #ab64965) or SRSF2 antibody (Abcam, #ab11826) diluted in 2% BSA buffer. The following day, cells were washed several times with PBS and incubated with the appropriate secondary antibody for 1 hour at room temperature. After extensive washing, the nuclei were stained with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole for 10 min. The coverslips were mounted, and images were captured using a Nikon A1RSi + confocal microscope equipped with a 100× oil immersion (numerical aperture, 1.45) objective. For analysis of puncta counts, thresholding was applied in ImageJ to create a mask of the nuclei. Then, using “Analyze Particles” to detect contiguous objects and exclude those touching the image edges, the remaining ones was added to the region of interest (ROI) Manager. Next, the nuclei were selected from the ROI Manager while the puncta-stained image is active. We used “Process > Find Maxima” to count the puncta in each selected nucleus. Two-sided
t

Recombinant protein purification
To purify RPB1 CTD, we fused the His × 6 and HA tag with 52 × CTD and cloned them into pET28a vector. The plasmid was transformed into Transetta (DE3)
Escherichia coli
chemically competent cells, and the recombinant proteins were produced in the presence of 200 nM isopropyl-β-
d
-thiogalactopyranoside for 18 hours at 16°C. Then, cells were collected and lysed with sonication (12-min duration, 2-s on/4-s off, 35% amplitude) in binding buffer [20 mM tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 300 mM NaCl, and 10 mM imidazole]. After centrifugation, the lysate was incubated with Ni–nitrilotriacetic acid agarose at 4°C with rotation for 1 hour. After washing with wash buffer [20 mM tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 300 mM NaCl, and 20 mM imidazole], the recombinant proteins were eluted with elution buffer [20 mM tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 300 mM NaCl, and 250 mM imidazole]. Also, the imidazole was removed using ultrafiltration spin columns, and the recombinant proteins were stored in storage buffer [20 mM tris-HCl (pH 7.5) and 150 mM NaCl].
To purify CLK1, CLK4, YES1, and CDK7, the cDNAs of these kinases were fused with Strep and Flag tag and cloned into pcDNA3.1(+) vector. The plasmids were transfected into HEK293F cells and incubated with shaking at 37°C for 72 hours, respectively. Cells were collected and lysed with lysis buffer [100 mM tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, and 1% NP-40 with 1× protease inhibitor] at 4°C for 1 hour. After centrifugation, the lysate was incubated with Strep beads (Smart-Lifesciences, #SA053005) for another 1 hour at 4°C. Then, the beads were washed with washing buffer [100 mM tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 150 mM NaCl, and 0.5% NP-40] and eluted with elution buffer [25 mM tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 150 mM NaCl, and 0.02% NP-40 with 10 mM desthiobiotin]. Then proteins were concentrated using ultrafiltration spin columns and stored in a storage buffer.
In vitro phosphorylation assay
The in vitro phosphorylation assay was preformed similarly as previous reported with some modifications (
94
). Briefly, the concentration of kinases and CTD was calculated using bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay kit (Beyotime, #P0010S). A 2 μg of kinase was incubated in kinase buffer [50 mM tris-HCl (pH 7.5) and 10 mM MgCl
2
] with or without inhibitor treatment (10 μM TG003 for CLK1 and CLK4 at 22°C, 10 μM CH6953755 for YES1 at 30°C, and 1 μM SY-5609 for CK7 at 30°C) for 1 hour with shaking. Then, 2 mM adenosine 5′-triphosphate and 5 μg of recombinant CTD were added and further incubated for 16 hours with shaking at indicated temperature, respectively. Then, 2× loading buffer was directly added to the mixture, and the reaction was terminated with boiling at 95°C for 10 min. The samples were subjected to reducing SDS-PAGE electrophoresis, and Western blotting was performed to detect the phosphorylation of CTD using specific antibodies.
Dot blot assay
CTD (YSPTSPS), pS5 CTD (YSPTS{P}PS), and pS5 CTD carrying T4V mutation (YSPVS{P}PS) heptapeptides were synthesized in GenScript, and the powder of peptides was dissolved in PBS. The in vitro dot blot assay was performed according to previously published protocol (
95
). Briefly, nitrocellulose membrane (0.45 μm) was incubated with 1% glutaraldehyde for 10 min at room temperature and then air-dried. Peptide samples at the indicated concentrations were spotted (1 μl per dot) onto the membrane and air-dried again. The membrane was then blocked with 2% BSA in TBST [20 mM tris-HCl, 150 mM NaCl, and 0.1% Tween 20 (pH 8.0)] for 30 min at room temperature, after which antibody incubation and detection were performed as in the Western blot procedure.
FACS-based CRISPR screening
A549 CRISPR KO library cells were derived from PKU-EdiGene High-Throughput Screening Core, which include 233,368 sgRNAs targeting 19,114 genes and 4000 nontarget sgRNAs (three sgRNAs and four barcodes per gene). For sample treatment, 1 × 10
8
cells (1000× coverage) were collected, and the subsequent procedures were similar to the “Chromatin fractionation for flow cytometry” section. After resuspend cells in PBS, cells were selected with FACS. The top 30% with the highest signals and bottom 30% with the lowest signals cell populations were collected, and their genomic DNA were extracted with phenol-chloroform method, respectively. For library construction, all extracted genomic DNAs were amplified with KAPA HIFI HS RM (Roche, #KK2602) with 3 μg DNA per reaction. Then, all the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) products were mixed thoroughly, and 500 μl of products was purified with DNA Clean & Concentrator (Zymo Research, #D4033). A 500 ng of purified PCR products was further purified with 1× Ampure beads (Beckman Coulter, #A63880). Final purified PCR products were subjected to library construction using the VAHTS Universal Pro DNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (Vazyme, #ND608). Sequencing was conducted using the Illumina platform by Annoroad, employing the PE150 sequencing strategy to generate 150–base pair (bp) paired-end sequencing reads.
Validation of CRISPR screening
The validation of the CRISPR screening was performed by independently generating KO cell lines and analyzing them by flow cytometry. The procedures for KO cell line construction and flow cytometry analysis were described in detail in the “Plasmids and cell lines construction”, “Lentivirus production and infection” and “Chromatin fractionation for flow cytometry” sections. In parallel to constructing the KO cell lines, we also transduced A549 Cas9 cells with a nontargeting sgRNA as a negative control. The sequences of the nontargeting sgRNA and the sgRNAs used for gene KO are listed in table S7. For each experiment, each sgRNA was tested in three biological replicates. For each KO cell line targeting a specific locus, we measured the median fluorescence signal of these cells and compared this to the median fluorescence signal of the negative control (nontargeting sgRNA) cells. If the ratio was >1, we interpreted it as indicating that KO at that locus increased phosphorylation at the corresponding site; if the ratio was <1, the KO was considered to have decreased phosphorylation. The Pearson’s correlation coefficient was calculated between the NormZ of CRISPR screening and the ratios derived from validation across the tested loci. The
P
value was calculated based on Pearson’s correlation test.
PolyA RNA-seq
For RNA extraction, the WT RNAPII was replaced with RNAPII mutants by treating cells with Dox (2 μg/ml) for 24 hours and 100 nM dTAGV-1 for 12 hours. Cells were seeded at equal density in six-well plates 24 hours before the experiment, with an additional plate used for cell counting. During the experiment, the culture medium was removed, and cells were lysed with 500 μl of TRIzol (Ambion, #15596018) reagent. After thorough lysis, the cell lysates were transferred to 1.5-ml centrifuge tubes, and 10% S2 cells was added as spike-in control. Chloroform was then added at a volume of

The aqueous phase was transferred to a new tube, and an equal volume of isopropanol was added, followed by incubation at room temperature for 10 min. The RNA was precipitated by centrifugation at 12,000 rpm for 15 min at 4°C, washed with 75% ethanol, and resuspended in diethyl pyrocarbonate (DEPC)–treated water. The samples were then sent to Annoroad for library construction and sequencing on the HiSeq-PE150 platform.

Transient transcriptome sequencing
To capture nascent RNA for sequencing, the WT RNAPII was replaced with RNAPII mutants by treating cells with Dox (2 μg/ml) for 24 hours and 100 nM dTAGV-1 for 4 hours. A final concentration of 1 mM 4-thiouridine (4SU, Macklin, #T820213) was added for 15-cm dishes of A549 cells labeling, and the cells were incubated in the dark for 30 min. After labeling, the cells were immediately treated with TRIzol reagent, and the lysates were collected into centrifuge tubes and stored at −80°C. For spike-in control, S2 cells were labeled with 100 μM 4SU labeled for 12 hours, and 10% labeled S2 cells was added to each sample. Total RNA was extracted, and the RNA was dissolved in two separate tubes containing 400 μl of DEPC water. After incubating at 65°C for 10 min to denature the RNA, the samples were sonicated using the Bioruptor plus (30-s on/30-s off, 10 cycles). Following a second incubation at 65°C for 10 min and a 5-min cooling period on ice, 6 μl of biotinylation buffer [833 mM tris-HCl (pH 7.4) and 83.3 mM EDTA] and 100 μl of MTSEA-Biotin (APExBIO, #A02-C5669)/

After phenol-chloroform extraction, the RNA was resuspended in 100 μl of DEPC-treated water. Then, 30 μl of Dynabeads M-280 Streptavidin beads (Invitrogen, #11205D) were added and incubated at room temperature for 30 min. After incubation, the beads were washed twice with 500 μl of prechilled high-salt wash buffer [50 mM tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 2 M NaCl, and 0.5% Triton X-100], followed by two washes with 500 μl of binding buffer [10 mM tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 300 mM NaCl, and 0.1% Triton X-100], and one wash with 500 μl of low-salt wash buffer [5 mM tris-HCl (pH 7.4) and 0.1% Triton X-100]. The supernatant was removed, and the new RNA was eluted in 300 μl of TRIzol reagent. The RNA was extracted, and cDNA libraries were prepared using the VAHTS Universal V8 RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (Vazyme, #NR605) with strand-specific sequencing. Sequencing was conducted using the Illumina platform by Annoroad, employing the PE150 sequencing strategy to generate 150-bp paired-end sequencing reads.
CUT&Tag
For CUT&Tag experiment, the WT RNAPII was replaced with RNAPII mutants by treating cells with Dox (2 μg/ml) for 24 hours and 100 nM dTAGV-1 for 4 hours. Cells were mixed with 10% mESCs cells and fixed with 0.1% formaldehyde, incubating at room temperature for 2 min. Crosslinking was terminated by the addition of 0.125 M glycine, and the samples were used for the CUT&Tag experiment following the Hyperactive Universal CUT&Tag Assay Kit for Illumina (Vazyme, #TD903) protocol. Briefly, after activation of ConA beads, 95 μl of wash buffer was added to the samples and incubated for 10 min on a rotator at room temperature. Histone H2A.Z antibody (Abcam, #ab4174) were then added and incubated overnight at 4°C. After secondary antibody incubation, samples were mixed with pA/G-Tnp for 1 hour on a rotator. Subsequently, the samples were tagmented in 40 μl of fragmentation buffer at 37°C for 1 hour. Following the manufacturer’s instructions, DNA was extracted and dissolved in 20 μl of nuclease-free water. To amplify the libraries, P5/P7 primers (Vazyme, #TD202) and 2× CAM PCR mix were added, and PCR was performed. PCR clean-up was conducted using DNA clean beads, and the libraries were eluted in 20 μl of nuclease-free water. Sequencing was conducted using the Illumina platform by Annoroad, employing the PE150 sequencing strategy to generate 150-bp paired-end sequencing reads.

Subcellular fractionation
The subcellular fractionation of cytosol, nucleoplasm, and chromatin was similar to ChIP-seq section. Briefly, 1 × 10
6
cells were collected and lysed on ice for 5 min using NP-40 lysis buffer [10 mM tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 150 mM NaCl, and 0.05% NP-40] containing 1× protease inhibitor (Roche, #04693132001). After centrifugation, the supernatant was collected as cytosol fraction. The pellet was resuspended in glycerol buffer [20 mM tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 75 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM EDTA, 0.85 mM DTT, and 50% glycerol] and incubated with nuclear lysis buffer [10 mM Hepes (pH 7.6), 7.5 mM MgCl
2
, 0.2 mM EDTA, 0.3 mM NaCl, 1 M urea, 1 mM DTT, and 1% NP-40] on ice for 2 min. After centrifugation, the supernatant was collected as the nucleoplasm fraction, and the pallets were identified as chromatin fraction. The three fractions were adjusted to the same volume, and 2× loading buffer was added.
CRISPR screening data analysis
Raw sequencing reads were counted with “library_count_sgrna_with_barcode” function in Mageck-ibar software (
96
). Also, the raw sgRNA counts with different barcodes were separated into four replicates with custom R script and subjected to DrugZ analysis (
97
). Differential sgRNA representation between the high-signal groups and the low-signal groups were compared, and a normalized
z
score (NormZ) was generated for each gene. Significant changed sgRNAs were identified with a cutoff of |NormZ| > 2 and
P
value < 0.01. All the significant changed sgRNAs from six screenings were merged together to generate RNAPII regulators. For clustering analysis,
k
-means algorithm was used to generate nine gene clusters according to NormZ score.
Poly(A) RNA-seq data analysis
The raw fastq files obtained from sequencing were first trimmed using Trim_galore (v.0.6.2) to remove adapter sequences, and quality control was performed with fastQC (v.0.11.8). The trimmed reads were aligned to a concatenated index of human (hg38) and
Drosophila melanogaster
(dm6) genome using STAR (v.2.7.3a), and PCR duplicates were removed using SAMtools (v.1.10). featureCounts (v.2.0.1) was used to summarize gene-level read counts per sample from the GENCODE annotation (v45). Reads in each gene were normalized as transcripts per million (TPM) to represent gene expression, and genes with TPM > 1 were used for correlation analysis. Pearson’s correlation coefficients were calculated in untreated groups of RNAPII
mut
WT, Y1F, S2A, T4V, S5A, and S7A cells. Significances were calculated on the basis of these coefficients. Differential gene expression analysis was performed using the DESeq2 (v.1.24.0) package in R, and dm6 reads were used for spike-in normalization. Differential expressed genes were determined using a cutoff of |log
2
(fold change)| > 1 and false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05.
ChIP-seq and CUT&Tag data analysis
Sequenced reads were processed by trimming adapter sequences using trim_galore (v.0.6.2), followed by quality assessment with FastQC (v.0.11.8). For endogenous RNAPII antibody ChIP-seq, reads were mapped to hg38 index, and for RNAPII
mut
ChIP-seq, H3K36me3 ChIP-seq, H2A.Zac ChIP-seq, and H2A.Z CUT&Tag, the reads were aligned to a concatenated index of human (hg38) and mouse (mm10) genomes using Bowtie2 (v.2.2.3). The resulting SAM files were converted to BAM format using SAMtools (v.1.10), followed by sorting, indexing, and removal of PCR duplicates with sambamba (v.0.7.1). Data visualization was conducted using DeepTools (v.3.3.1). Specifically, biological replicates were merged using the samtools merge function, and the combined BAM files were converted into BigWig format via the bamCoverage function. For RNAPII
mut
ChIP-seq, reads mapped to mouse genome were used to calculate the scaling factor, and for other experiments, Reads Per Genomic Content (RPGC) method was used to normalize the BigWig file. To compare the chromatin binding of proximal promoter (−2000 to +300 bp of TSS), gene body (+300 bp of TSS to TES), and termination region (TES to +2000 bp of TES) in RNAPII
mut
ChIP-seq, multibigwigsummary was used to summarize the coverage of these regions based on specific bed files. Two-sided Wilcoxon tests were used to calculate significances between WT and other RNAPII
mut
groups to visualize gene occupancy, the computeMatrix function was used to analyze read distribution across target regions, and the plotProfile function was used to generate corresponding plots. Narrow peaks for two biological replicates were called using MACS2 (v.2.2.7.1) with cutoff of
q
< 0.05, respectively, and two peak files were merged with IDR (v2.0.4.2).
For NMF analysis, multibigwigsummary method was used to quantify densities of RNAPII, pY1, pS2, pT4, pS5, and pS7 ChIP-seq on protein coding genes. Two replicates were summarized, and a threshold of twofold enrichment over input was applied to identify candidate genes for downstream analysis. All signals within each group were normalized using
z
-score transformation and shifted to ensure all values were positive. Then, R package NMF (v. 0.22.0) was used to perform NMF analysis according to the manufacturers’ instructions. Three modules were identified, and genes with the highest metagene scores were assigned to the corresponding module.
For traveling ratio, transcription efficiency, and read through index calculation, ChIP-seq densities of proximal promoter, gene body, and termination region were first summarized for each RNAPII mutant with DeepTools (v.3.3.1) using bigwigCompare function according to GENCODE annotation (v45). Then, traveling ratio, transcription efficiency, and read through index were calculated with proximal promoter dividing gene body, termination region dividing proximal promoter, and termination region dividing gene body for each gene, respectively. Limma (v.3.40.6) package was then used for differential analysis, following the manufacturer’s instruction. A cutoff of fold change> 1.5 and FDR < 0.01 was used to identify significant changed genes.
For CLK1, CLK4, and YES1 binding genes identification, MACS2 (v.2.2.7.1) was used to call peaks with cutoff of
q
value < 0.05 for two biological replicates, respectively. Then, the overlapped peaks of two replicates were obtained using bedtools intersect function with minimal overlap of 50% for each peak. Then, peaks were annotated with ChIPseeker (v.1.5.1) to their nearest genes. Then, the fragments per kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads (FPKM) of each peak was calculated, and genes with top 500 peaks were identified as the binding genes.
TT-seq data analysis
TT-seq analyses followed a similar approach to polyadenylate [poly(A)] RNA-seq with some modifications. Trimmed reads were mapped to the concatenated hg38-dm6 genome index with STAR (v.2.7.3a). Replicate BAM files were merged with the samtools merge function, and the merged BAM files were converted into BigWig files using the bamCoverage function. The TPM of RPB1 gene in RNAPII WT replacement cell and
D. melanogaster
(dm6) reads were used together to calculate spike-in normalization factor. To differentiate between sense and antisense strands, the bamCoverage function was applied with the “-filterRNAstrand” parameter set to forward or reverse. The visualization of genome-wide distributions was performed using DeepTools (v.3.3.1). The computeMatrix function was used to calculate read distribution across target regions, and the plotHeatmap function was used to generate meta-gene plots. To quantify gene expression, multibigwigsummary was used to summarize TT-seq signals on active genes, lncRNAs and snRNAs, respectively. Two-sided Wilcoxon tests were used to calculate significances between untreated and RNAPII
mut
groups. RNAPII
mut
TT-seq signaling dividing ChIP-seq was used to generate RNAPII velocity as described previously (
98
).
To identify mutant preferentially and RPB1
dTAG
constitutive down-regulated genes, the TT-seq [Log
2
(fold change) < −1.5] and RNA-seq [log
2
(fold change) < −2] overlapped down-regulated genes of RPB1
dTAG
and RNAPII
mut
cells were classified as transcriptional down-regulated genes. For each RNAPII
mut
cells, the transcriptional down-regulated genes, which were overlapped with transcriptional down-regulated genes of RPB1
dTAG
cells, were identified as RPB1
dTAG
constitutive down-regulted genes, and those that were not overlapped with RPB1
dTAG
cells were identified as mutant preferentially down-regulated genes. To identify active genes in A549 cells, the TPM values for untreated cells were calculated and genes with mean TPM > 1 (
n
= 9958) were defined as active genes.
Quantitative ChIP-MS data analysis
Statistical analyses of proteomic data were conducted using the DEqMS R package (v.1.2.0), following the manufacturer’s guidelines. Missing values were imputed with MinProb function from MSnbase package (v.2.10.1). Also, data were normalized with library size. For endogenous RNAPII antibody ChIP-MS, IgG group is used as control group, and a cutoff of FDR < 0.05 and log
2
(fold change) > 1 was set to identify significant enriched proteins. Enriched protein from six endogenous RNAPII antibody ChIP-MS was merged to generate RNAPII regulators. For RNAPII
mut
ChIP-MS, paired comparisons between different mutants and WT cells were performed, and a filter threshold of FDR < 0.05 and |log
2
(fold change)> 1 was used to identify differential proteins for each mutant.
Gene functional enrichment analysis
GO enrichment analysis was conducted using Metascape (
https://metascape.org/
) (
99
) with relevant gene sets. For annotation of cancer hallmarks, datasets were downloaded from COSMIC database (
https://cancer.sanger.ac.uk/census
). Genes with hallmarks features were kept for downstream analysis. The classification of these genes is similar to previously reported based on GO terms (
100
).
Kinase motif analysis
Motif score data were derived from published data for serine/threonine and tyrosine kinase, respectively (
78
,
79
). Motif score of RNAPII CTD for each kinase was selected and subsequently divided into Y1, S2, T4, S5, and S7 phosphorylation site according to amino acid sequences. The max motif score of selected kinase on specific phosphorylation sites was used as the motif score for selected kinase. The kinase motif data was derived from Kinase Logos (
https://esbl.nhlbi.nih.gov/Databases/Kinase_Logos/
) (
101
), and web Logo (
https://weblogo.berkeley.edu/logo.cgi
) was used to create motif logos (
102
,
103
).
Statistical analysis
For cell proliferation assay, FACS, RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, CUT&Tag, TT-seq, and ChIP-MS, at least two biological replicates were performed.
P
values and statistical tests were noted in individual figure legends and corresponding methods sections. All data processing and statistical tests were performed in R (v.3.6.1) or GraphPad Prism (v.10.4.0). Custom codes for statistical analysis were available upon requests.
body:
INTRODUCTION
The C-terminal domain (CTD) of RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) comprises 52 repeats of the heptapeptide YSPTSPS in mammalian cells (
1
–
3
). Phosphorylation of the CTD at five specific sites (pY1, pS2, pT4, pS5, and pS7) is well-documented and is known to be associated with transcription and cotranscriptional events, including RNA processing and modulation of the chromatin landscape (
4
–
7
). Genomic mapping from various studies has shown that pS2 and pT4 are enriched in gene body regions, while other phosphorylation sites are enriched in promoter-proximal regions. The most extensively studied sites, pS5 and pS2, are linked to early transcription and elongation stages, respectively. pY1 is associated with antisense promoter transcription and transcriptional termination (
8
–
11
). pT4 is implicated in chromatin remodeling in yeast and the regulation of 3′ end RNA processing (
12
–
14
), and pS7 seems to regulate small nuclear RNA (snRNA) transcription (
15
,
16
). However, comprehensive comparative analyses of these five phosphorylation sites, their chromatin occupancy, protein interaction partners, and their roles in transcription and cotranscriptional regulation are still lacking in the field.
Previous studies in mammalian cells or yeast have identified a number of kinases—including CDK7, CDK9, CDK12, GSK-3, Hrr25, PLK3 and SLT2—and phosphatases such as SSU72, CTDP1 (FCP1), PP1/PNUTS, Glc7, and Rtr1, which are known to regulate the phosphorylation of the RNAPII (
17
–
32
). The phosphorylation status of the RNAPII is crucial for various cellular processes, particularly during development and in the context of diseases (
33
,
34
). Consequently, it is plausible that many unidentified signaling or regulatory pathways may modulate cell states during development or disease by influencing RNAPII phosphorylation. Specifically, the “orphan” residues Y1, T4, and S7—whose potential functions, corresponding kinases, and phosphatases remain largely unknown—may contribute to specialized roles in RNAPII-mediated gene expression (
35
,
36
). Expanding the list of RNAPII phosphorylation regulators, especially those associated with specific diseases, could offer insights into disease mechanisms and potentially lead to the development of targeted inhibitors (
37
,
38
).
In this study, we first validated specific antibodies for the phosphorylation of the RNAPII. We characterized five RNAPII phosphorylation sites, identifying 706 candidate interactors, and showed that their genomic occupancy sites were associated with diverse genetic and epigenetic features. In addition, we conducted a CRISPR–fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) screen, revealing 2067 potential regulators of RNAPII phosphorylation, which include 79 cancer hallmark genes, 94 kinases, and 21 phosphatases. Among these were known regulators and many previously unreported ones. Furthermore, we rapidly replaced the wild-type (WT) RNAPII with mutants containing mutated phosphorylation sites and found that these mutations influence various transcriptional processes and preferentially alter histone modifications. Together, we decoded the features, regulatory networks, and functions associated with five distinct sites on RNAPII CTD in human cells. Moreover, FeaSion serves as a powerful platform technology for elucidating the site-specific “Features-Regulators-Functions” network, making it broadly applicable for investigating modifications beyond phosphorylation and proteins beyond RNA polymerases.
RESULTS
FeaSion strategy identifies phosphorylated RNAPII Features, Screening regulators and mutant function
RNAPII CTD phosphorylation sites included pY1, pS2, pT4, pS5 and pS7, which had been studied, primarily in individual. In this study, we planned to implement the FeaSion strategy to obtain features of all five sites of phosphorylated RNAPII, screen regulators, and investigate mutant effects in mammalian cells (
Fig. 1A
). We anticipated that this approach would allow us to simultaneously compare the features of these phosphorylation sites using validated specific antibodies. We leveraged CRISPR screening alongside fluorescently labeled RNAPII phosphorylation antibodies to quantify fluorescent signals using FACS. Increases or decreases in fluorescent signal intensity indicated negative or positive candidate regulators of RNAPII phosphorylation. To investigate the functional roles of RNAPII phosphorylation, we first introduced the RPB1
dTAG
into A549 cells, which could be degraded upon the addition of degrader of Tag, von Hippel–Lindau ligand 1 (dTAGV-1). Next, we knocked out the endogenous RNAPII subunit B1 (RPB1) and subsequently introduced Tet-on expressed hemagglutinin (HA)–tagged RPB1 containing either WT or various phosphorylation mutants (Y1F, S2A, T4V, S5A, and S7A). Transcriptome and chromatin landscape analyses following the rapid replacement of WT RPB1 with phosphorylation mutants would reveal the immediate site-specific functions of RNAPII CTD.

B

C
) Heatmap showing the NMF clustering results of RNAPII, pY1, pS2, pT4, pS5, and pS7 ChIP-seq signals on protein coding genes. The color indicated the relative enrichment efficiency of each cluster in each ChIP-seq replicate. (
D

E
) Scatter plot (left) illustrating the relationship between TPM values of 1635 TFs and their genomic distances to the nearest super enhancers in A549 cells. Master TFs were defined as those within the top 10% of gene expression levels and located within 5 kb of a super-enhancer. Box plot (right) comparing the expression levels of master TFs versus other TFs. Statistical significance was assessed by a two-sided Wilcoxon test. ***
P
< 0.001. (

) Metagene profiles of FOSL2 (left), MYC (middle), and BCL3 (right) ChIP-seq signals on three modules of genes in A549 cells.
We used previously documented RNAPII phosphorylation antibodies to conduct chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) and ChIP–mass spectrometry (MS) analyses (tables S1 and S2). We performed immunoprecipitation using each antibody (pY1, pS2, pT4, pS5, and pS7), followed by immunoblotting with the full panel of phosphorylation-specific antibodies by using the total RNAPII as the loading control. In these experiments, we consistently observed that each antibody showed the strongest reactivity toward its corresponding phosphorylation form, which supports their site specificity. At the same time, signals corresponding to other phosphorylation forms were also detected in the precipitated material (fig. S1A). This observation is consistent with the concept that individual RNAPII molecules often carry multiple phosphorylation marks concurrently during transcription. This multiplexed phosphorylation of the CTD heptad repeats has been well documented. For instance, pT4 pS5 double phosphorylation sites occurring exclusively during the transcription of protein-coding genes (
39
). Together, both our data and the literature strongly indicate that, while each antibody shows strong and specific binding to its own epitope, the detection of additional phosphorylation signals is reflective of the physiological reality.
As observed in previous studies, pS2 and pT4 were preferentially enriched in gene bodies, while pY1, pS5, pS7, and total RNAPII (N-terminal domain, NTD) were predominantly localized to promoter-proximal regions (
Fig. 1B
and fig. S1B). The ChIP-MS data were highly reproducible (fig. S1C), with many proteins identified aligning with findings from different studies (fig. S1, D and E) (
40
,
41
). The proteins identified through ChIP-MS largely overlap and are enriched in transcriptional processes (fig. S1F). Through clustering analyses, we identified specific protein clusters that preferentially associated with total RNAPII (cluster 1), all forms of RNAPII (cluster 2), and distinct clusters enriched for pS2 and pS5 (cluster 3) or pY1, pT4, and pS7 (cluster 4) (fig. S1G). Gene Ontology (GO) analyses indicated that these clusters were enriched in various functional pathways, including RNAPII transcription, stem cell population maintenance, SUMOylation, and autophagy (fig. S1H).
To further explore the features associated with CTD phosphorylation of RNAPII, we first performed NMF (non-negative matrix factorization) clustering analysis, which identified three distinct modules enriched in total RNAPII, pY1 and pS5 (module 1), pS2 (module 2), and pT4 (module 3) (
Fig. 1C
). We observed that module 2 was enriched for genes with a higher number of exons, increased chromatin accessibility, and elevated H3K36me3 levels. In contrast, module 3 was characterized by genes with greater gene length, higher expression levels, elevated H3K27ac levels, and relatively lower m6A levels. Notably, DNA methylation and RNA half-life did not exhibit notable differences across the three modules (
Fig. 1D
and fig. S1, I and J). We then defined active transcription events proximal to super-enhancers as master transcription factors (TFs) in our cellular context and found that these master TFs generally exhibited higher expression levels and were associated with cancer cell growth (
Fig. 1E
) (
42
,
43
). For master TFs with available ChIP-seq binding data in our cell system, we observed preferential enrichment of FOS like 2 (FOSL2) in module 3, while MYC showed reduced enrichment in module 1. This pattern is reminiscent of MYC’s established role in RNAPII pause-release regulation (
44
). In contrast, B-cell lymphoma 3 protein (BCL3) did not display a clear preference across the three modules (
Fig. 1F
). Collectively, these findings suggest that CTD phosphorylation of RNAPII is associated with various transcriptional features, which may be regulated by multiple signaling pathways at diverse environmental stimuli.
CRISPR screening identifies thousands of candidate regulators that preferentially modulate different RNAPII phosphorylation sites
We optimized a previously published FACS protocol to quantify chromatin-associated RNAPII phosphorylation signals (
Fig. 2A
) (
45
,
46
). This was achieved by permeabilizing the cells before performing immunofluorescent labeling with antibodies specific to phosphorylated RNAPII or total RNAPII. To validate this protocol, we assessed phosphorylated histone H3 serine 10 (H3pS10) and RNAPII antibody using FACS. H3pS10 is a well-established chromatin modification that marks mitotic cells and is widely used in flow cytometry to identify mitosis (
47
,
48
). During mitosis, global transcription is halted, and transcription-associated proteins, including RNAPII, are largely displaced from chromatin (
49
–
51
). Permeabilization removes unbound or loosely chromatin-associated proteins while leaving tightly chromatin-bound proteins largely intact (
52
). Accordingly, the dissociation of RNAPII from chromatin during mitosis is detectable only in permeabilized cells—not in nonpermeabilized samples—as demonstrated by our flow cytometry data and supported by Bay
et al
. (
46
). In contrast, H3pS10 is an integral component of mitotic chromosomes, which is why its immunofluorescence signal remains unaffected by permeabilization (
Fig. 2B
). Furthermore, the immunofluorescence experiment confirmed the nuclear localization of RNAPII in nonmitotic permeabilized cells (fig. S2A). To further verify the specificity of phosphorylated RNAPII antibodies, we conducted FACS quantification, which revealed specific distributions compared to immunoglobulin G (IgG) signals (fig. S2B); these RNAPII fluorescent signals could be further suppressed using various RNAPII phosphorylation inhibitors (fig. S2, C to F).

Leveraging the advantages of FACS quantification for phosphorylated RNAPII, we performed CRISPR screening to select the top 30% and bottom 30% of fluorescent signals. Genes whose knockout (KO) reduced RNAPII levels were defined as positive candidate regulators, while those increased RNAPII levels were defined as negative candidate regulators. We used genome-wide CRISPR stable KO cells, which may result in the missing of essential regulators from our screening. By normalizing the signals of input cells, we can effectively exclude potential interference from cell growth. We extracted genomic DNA from these cells and sequenced the single guide RNAs (sgRNAs). A total of six CRISPR screens (total RNAPII, pY1, pS2, pT4, pS5, and pS7) were conducted in A549 cells, with four replicates clustered together in principal components analysis analyses (fig. S2G). We applied stringent cutoffs to the CRISPR screening data and identified candidate regulators for RNAPII phosphorylation (table S3). The results showed that nontargeting controls remained unchanged (
Fig. 2C
), while several reported regulators of RNAPII phosphorylation were shown up in our screen (
Fig. 2D
) (
19
,
23
,
53
–
66
). Although some candidates did not appear in our plots, they still influenced outcomes despite not match our stringent cutoff criteria. Correlation analysis indicated a high correlation between candidate regulators of pY1 and pS7 (fig. S2H). By comparing the regulators of RNAPII NTD, we can identify potential regulators for the specific phosphorylation sites on the RNAPII. The upset plots from RNAPII phosphorylation analyses revealed that many factors clustered within specific categories of RNAPII phosphorylation sites (
Fig. 2E
). Clustering analyses suggested that positive regulators appeared to exhibit relatively specific patterns in regulating particular RNAPII phosphorylation sites—for instance, DNA repair and mRNA transcription for total RNAPII and amino acid transport and G protein–coupled receptor signaling for pS5 (
Fig. 2, F and G
). These diverse functional pathways associated with specific RNAPII phosphorylation sites merit further investigation in future studies.
Candidate regulators associated with RNAPII phosphorylation are linked to cancer hallmarks
Cancer cells typically exhibit an accelerated growth rate and rely on dysregulated transcriptional activities (
67
–
69
). In total, 2067 candidate regulators were identified; notably, 79 of these overlap with cancer hallmarks, which collectively include 344 cancer hallmark genes from the Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (COSMIC) database (
Fig. 2H
). Among the overlapping cancer hallmarks, we observed significant enrichment in categories such as evading growth suppressors, activating invasion, sustaining proliferative signals, and resisting cell death. We independently validated these cancer hallmark genes and many other candidate regulators using FACS and CRISPR KO techniques (
Fig. 2I
). Among these, 112 genes (94.1%) recapitulated the phenotypic trends observed in the primary screen—a validation rate consistent with those reported in comparable studies [e.g., 91.0% in (
70
), 96.3% in (
71
), 61.5% in (
72
), and 96.1% in (
73
)]. Furthermore, we observed a decent Pearson’s correlation (
r
= 0.805) between the CRISPR screening scores and validation outcomes (
Fig. 2J
), underscoring the robustness of our dataset. Cytoscape analyses of the protein complexes identified through CRISPR screening revealed that these candidate regulators are enriched in processes related to transcription, histone modifications, signal transduction, proteasome-mediated protein degradation, RNA splicing, and DNA replication (fig. S2I). Many of these candidate regulators have been associated with human diseases in the literature. Collectively, these analyses suggest that RNAPII phosphorylation candidate regulators are linked to various diseases, providing insights into disease mechanisms and potential treatment strategies.
RNAPII phosphorylation site mutants affect various transcriptional processes
To investigate the functions of RNAPII phosphorylation, we acutely degraded WT RPB1 and replaced it with various phosphorylation site mutants using wildtype as a control. Western blot analyses indicated that the addition of dTAGV-1 rapidly degraded the WT RPB1, which is green fluorescent protein (GFP)–tagged (
Fig. 3A
). Following the addition of doxycycline (Dox), we induced the expression of various RPB1 phosphorylation site mutants. The RNAPII N-terminal antibodies recognized all forms of RNAPII, and the protein signals in lanes 1 and 4 of
Fig. 3A
, examined with the RNAPII NTD antibodies, suggested that the replacement RPB1 mutants were expressed at similar levels to WT RPB1. Immunofluorescence analyses revealed that these phosphorylation site mutants localized in the nucleus and interacted with other RNAPII subunits, as confirmed by MS analyses (
Fig. 3, B and C
). Gene expression in these engineered cells was also highly correlated with WT cells, suggesting that the phosphorylation site mutants did not adversely affect the cells without the addition of Dox and dTAGV-1 (
Fig. 3D
). Correlation analyses of ChIP-MS data between endogenous RPB1 and the replaced WT RPB1 also showed high correlation. Together, these control experiments indicate that these engineered cells can be used to investigate the immediate functions of different phosphorylation sites of RNAPII.

Whether our CTD phosphorylation-site mutations truly mimic an unmodified CTD and whether they may affect phosphorylation at other sites were investigated. We first immunoprecipitated each HA-tagged RNAPII mutant and probed them with a comprehensive panel of CTD phospho-specific antibodies using WT RNAPII as a control (fig. S3A). As expected, each mutation abolished detection of its corresponding phospho-epitope, confirming the specific loss of phosphorylation at the targeted site. Notably, the Y1F mutation reduced levels of pS2 and pS7 relative to WT (0.30-fold and 0.33-fold of WT, respectively; normalized to total RNAPII), which aligns with previous reports that pY1 primes pS2 in mammalian cells (
74
). The S7A mutation eliminated pS7 while leaving phosphorylation at other sites largely unaffected (ranging from 0.85-fold to 1.08-fold of WT). By contrast, the S2A, T4V, and S5A mutations resulted in a near-complete loss of immunoreactivity across all phosphorylation-specific CTD antibodies. Furthermore, although the hyperphosphorylated form of RNAPII remained detectable in S2A and T4V mutants using an HA tag antibody targeting total RNAPII, it was abolished by the S5A mutation. An alternative explanation is that these mutations impair antibody binding by altering the epitope landscape, rather than abolishing phosphorylation of other sites. 20

13

Next, we explored the functions of RNAPII phosphorylation using mutants. Cell growth analyses demonstrated that the RNAPII phosphorylation site mutants showed marginal effects on the cell cycle but did influence cell growth (fig. 75

76

We then conducted RNAPII ChIP-MS for both WT and phosphorylation mutants, enabling us to identify proteins with altered differential interactions. Our systematic analysis identifies CLK1/4 and YES1 as specialized regulators of RNA polymerase II CTD phosphorylation
We conducted three categories of screenings to investigate the candidate regulators of RNAPII phosphorylation (table S5). The endogenous antibody ChIP-MS for RNAPII phosphorylation identified a total of 706 candidate factors interacting with RNAPII (fig. S5C). Following this, the analysis of preferentially changed proteins after RNAPII mutations revealed 1000 factors (fig. S5D), while CRISPR screening identified 2067 factors (fig. S5E). Among these three screenings, we found 37 overlapping factors. GO term analyses indicated that these shared factors were enriched in processes related to transcription, mRNA metabolism, and blastocyst development, among others (fig. S5C). Some of these factors are known regulators of RNAPII phosphorylation, while many remain unreported and warrant further investigation in the future.
As known RNAPII kinases and phosphatases are critical targets for drug design and play significant roles in many diseases, we believe that identifying additional RNAPII kinases and phosphatases is essential not only for understanding the regulation of RNAPII phosphorylation but also for elucidating disease mechanisms. We specifically analyzed the kinases and phosphatases identified through our various methodologies: feature analysis (ChIP-MS), screening (CRISPR KO), and functional studies (mutagenesis followed by ChIP-MS). The results indicated that most of the identified kinases are serine/threonine-specific, including CMGC kinases (CDKs, MAPKs, GSKs, and CLKs), SRC family kinases and others (
Fig. 6, A and B
). These kinases are enriched in the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase–AKT signaling, MAPK signaling, and transforming growth factor–β pathways. Subsets of these signaling regulators have been validated. Recent studies have investigated the in vitro activities of kinases (
78
,
79
). By integrating our CRISPR screening data, we identified DYRK1A, CLK1, CLK4, and YES1 as potential regulators of RNAPII phosphorylation (
Fig. 6C
and fig. S5G). Notably, DYRK1A has been demonstrated to regulate the phosphorylation at serine-2 of RNAPII CTD (
57
,
80
). Tyrosine kinase YES1 is amplified and overexpressed in many cancers, making it a significant drug target involved in signal transduction (
81
,
82
); however, its precise mechanisms in transcription remain elusive. Serine/threonine kinases CLK1/4 are considered promising targets for various human diseases due to their critical role in RNA splicing (
83
,
84
). Notably, YES1 was detected in both our RNAPII ChIP-MS and mutant ChIP-MS, while CLK1/4 was not detected in our ChIP-MS approach likely attributable to the limited ability of ChIP-MS to detect certain weak or transient interactions.

We next generated KO cells of CLK1, CLK4, or YES1 to investigate their roles in RNAPII phosphorylation. We confirmed that CLK1 or CLK4 KO reduced pS7 levels, while YES1 KO decreased pY1 levels, although to a lesser extent (
Fig. 6D
). Consistent with these findings, the CLK1/4 kinase inhibitor TG003 specifically reduced pS7 levels, whereas the inhibitor SRI-29329 appeared to affect RNAPII protein stability (fig. S6A). These results support the functional linkage between CLK1/4 and RNAPII, although some variations observed may stem from differences in perturbation strategies. In addition, YES1 KO or its chemical inhibitors consistently suppressed pY1 levels, as validated by Western blotting (
Fig. 6D
and fig. S6B).
To gain functional insights into RNAPII transcription, we performed RNAPII and pS7 ChIP-seq following CLK1/4 perturbation and RNAPII and pY1 ChIP-seq after YES1 perturbation (
Fig. 6, E and F
). The results demonstrated that CLK1/4 KO or TG003 treatment down-regulated pS7 and RNAPII chromatin occupancy, while YES1 KO reduced pY1 and RNAPII chromatin occupancy. Notably, the YES1 inhibitor CH6953755 down-regulated pY1. To minimize potential biases associated with high-dose inhibitor treatment, we further conducted ChIP-seq experiments after treatment with 1 μM TG003 or 1 μM CH6953755. Log
2
(fold change) heatmaps revealed that 1 μM TG003 preferentially decreased pS7 occupancy within gene bodies and transcription end site (TES) regions, while 20 μM TG003 resulted in a broader reduction across entire genes. Similarly, both 1 and 10 μM CH6953755 consistently reduced pY1 occupancy at transcription start site (TSS) regions (fig. S6C). These findings align with the phenotypic changes observed in CLK1/4 and YES1 KO cells, supporting the conclusion that the inhibitors specifically target CLK1/4 and YES1 activity, leading to reduced RNAPII pS7 and pY1 phosphorylation. Note that we also observed a small subset of genes showing slight increases upon KO and drug treatment; however, the vast majority of active genes exhibited decreased occupancy. These few upregulated cases are likely attributable to broader cellular responses rather than direct effects. Traveling ratio analyses further indicated that CLK4 and YES1 regulate transcription elongation, while CLK1 modulates transcription initiation in cells (fig. S6D). The overlap analyses of CLK1/4-affected genes and S7A mutant-affected genes, as well as YES1-affected genes and Y1F mutant-affected genes, indicate an overlap of ~50% (fig. S6E). This is consistent with the roles of CLK1/4 in S7 phosphorylation and YES1 in Y1 phosphorylation.
To provide direct evidence for CLK1/4 and YES1 in regulating RNAPII phosphorylation, we purified CLK1/4, YES1, and RNAPII CTD to establish an in vitro phosphorylation assay using purified CDK7 as a positive control (
Fig. 6, G and H
, and fig. S6F). The results revealed that CLK1 and CLK4 specifically phosphorylate RNAPII CTD at S2, T4, and S7, activities that were inhibited by their respective inhibitors. While S2 and T4 phosphorylation was not observed in cells, this discrepancy may arise from in vitro experimental conditions. In vitro assays also confirmed that YES1 specifically phosphorylates the Y1 site of RNAPII CTD. CDK7, as expected, phosphorylated all examined sites, consistent with its known promiscuity (fig. S6F). Furthermore, RNAPII immunoprecipitation confirmed physical interactions between RNAPII and CLK1/4 as well as YES1 (fig. S6G).
In addition to CLK1/4 and YES1, we also validated physical interactions between RNAPII and six kinases and phosphatases (ULK3, DUSP9, CAMK1D, PTPN14, ACVR2A, and MAP2K5) using co-immunoprecipitation assays. These interactions were initially identified via CRISPR screening but were either undetected or not significantly enriched in previous ChIP-MS experiments (fig. S6G).
To explore the chromatin-associated regulatory roles of CLK1/4 and YES1, we first confirmed their presence in chromatin fractions (fig. S6H). We then performed ChIP-seq experiments with CLK1/4 and YES1-specific antibodies using the respective KO cells as negative controls (
Fig. 6I
and table S6). This strategy significantly reduced background signals caused by nonspecific antibody binding, improving the reliability of identified chromatin-binding peaks. We then performed functional clustering of these KO-controlled peaks (
Fig. 6J
) and highlighted representative genomic loci (
Fig. 6K
). GO analysis indicated that peaks bound by CLK1/4 and YES1 were enriched in DNA-templated transcription, underscoring their roles in transcriptional regulation. Furthermore, CLK1/4 peaks were associated with RNA metabolism and developmental processes, suggesting involvement in both transcriptional and posttranscriptional regulation. YES1-bound peaks were linked to cell differentiation, migration, and response to stimuli, implying broader biological functions beyond transcription. At specific gene loci—
ING5
,
DLX2
, and
IMPACT
—we detected binding by all three kinases. Their KO resulted in reduced RNAPII occupancy and decreased phosphorylation signals at pS7 and pY1, consistent with the loss of kinase-specific binding at these regions.
Regarding genome-wide versus gene-specific regulation, our analyses demonstrate that CLK1/4 and YES1 bind to specific genomic loci (fig. S7, A to C). Genes lacking CLK1/4 or YES1 binding are generally transcriptionally inactive and exhibit low RNAPII occupancy. At kinase-bound genes, both pS7 and pY1 levels were significantly reduced upon KO. In addition, we also observed that KO of CLK1/4 or YES1 resulted in a broad decrease in pS7 and pY1 levels across all active genes (
Fig. 6, E and F
), indicating that the reduction of these marks occurs genome wide. These findings suggest that while CLK1/4 and YES1 binding is site-specific, their KO leads to a widespread loss of RNAPII phosphorylation. The prolonged absence of these kinases in stable KO cell lines may induce broader cellular adaptations, which could contribute to the observed global reduction in RNAPII binding and phosphorylation.
DISCUSSION
We characterized RNAPII phosphorylation by identifying 706 candidate interacting proteins. In addition, we identified 2067 potential regulators of RNAPII phosphorylation, of which 79 are recognized as hallmark cancer genes. Mutants of RNAPII phosphorylation preferentially affect transcriptional processes and histone modifications. Through integrative analyses of the extensive data generated in this study, we propose the concept of the CTD code of RNAPII, where different regulators modulate the distinct phosphorylation sites on the RNAPII CTD, with each site performing preferential functions in gene expression.
The site-specific functions of posttranslational modifications in key cellular components represent crucial regulatory mechanisms underlying biological activities. Furthermore, a comprehensive understanding of these site-specific regulations can unveil promising targets for precision medicine. Beyond phosphorylation, various protein translational modifications such as methylation, acetylation, and ubiquitination and other are known to play significant roles in cellular processes. In addition, there is a strong demand in this field to elucidate the site-specific features, regulators, and functions of posttranslational modifications in histones and other essential cellular components. In this study, we conducted an innovative investigation of RNAPII phosphorylation using the FeaSion strategy. We believe that our FeaSion platform lays a solid foundation for further exploration of the features, screening, and functions related to the site-specific actions of other critical cellular factors. The potential applications of this platform are vast and transformative, paving the way for advancements in molecular biology and therapeutic development.
Technically, our mutation strategy involved introducing substitutions at the corresponding residues across all 52 heptad repeats of the CTD, which increases complexity in a cellular context. Our immunoprecipitation and Western blot analyses revealed that mutations such as S2A, T4V, and S5A resulted in a near-complete loss of signal with phosphorylation-specific CTD antibodies. However, we acknowledge that these mutations may influence epitope accessibility and thus confound antibody-based detection. For accuracy, we have explicitly attributed the observed effects to the respective mutants (Y1F, S2A, T4V, S5A, and S7A) themselves.
The CRISPR screening identified thousands of candidate regulators of RNAPII phosphorylation; however, it does not directly indicate whether these candidates are involved in the regulation of RNAPII phosphorylation in a direct or indirect manner. Therefore, we conducted overlapping analyses of the candidate regulators that interact with the RNAPII complex or exhibit altered interaction strength after the mutation of RNAPII phosphorylation. Identifying kinases or phosphatases for RNAPII, as well as regulators for known kinases or phosphatases involved in RNAPII phosphorylation, requires more rigorous in vitro kinase activity assays and acute protein degradation followed immediate multi-omics analyses. In addition, we also could not exclude false positive hits for those unvalidated candidates from both CRISPR and MS screenings.
Our ChIP-MS method, which uses crosslinking followed by immunoprecipitation, captures both stable and strong interactions and a subset of dynamic and weaker associations. In contrast, proximity-labeling techniques such as TurboID and APEX are especially powerful for identifying highly transient or low-affinity interactions. While our ChIP-MS approach may not fully detect these weak or transit associations, proximity-labeling strategies offer a complementary avenue to achieve this. When combined with our CRISPR screening results, these orthogonal approaches hold strong potential to more comprehensively identify candidate regulators of RNAPII.
We found that many candidate regulators of RNAPII phosphorylation are hallmark cancer genes, with several also associated with human diseases. However, it remains unclear how these candidate regulators contribute to disease through dysregulation of RNAPII phosphorylation. Therefore, it is essential to conduct further screenings using other disease-relevant, drug target–sensitive, and resistant cell lines. Furthermore, performing additional CRISPR screenings across various cancer cell lines would provide specific candidates tailored to particular cancer types.

Validation of CRISPR screening
The validation of the CRISPR screening was performed by independently generating KO cell lines and analyzing them by flow cytometry. The procedures for KO cell line construction and flow cytometry analysis were described in detail in the “Plasmids and cell lines construction”, “Lentivirus production and infection” and “Chromatin fractionation for flow cytometry” sections. In parallel to constructing the KO cell lines, we also transduced A549 Cas9 cells with a nontargeting sgRNA as a negative control. The sequences of the nontargeting sgRNA and the sgRNAs used for gene KO are listed in table S7. For each experiment, each sgRNA was tested in three biological replicates. For each KO cell line targeting a specific locus, we measured the median fluorescence signal of these cells and compared this to the median fluorescence signal of the negative control (nontargeting sgRNA) cells. Two replicates were summarized, and a threshold of twofold enrichment over input was applied to identify candidate genes for downstream analysis. All signals within each group were normalized using
z
-score transformation and shifted to ensure all values were positive. Then, R package NMF (v. 0.22.0) was used to perform NMF analysis according to the manufacturers’ instructions. Three modules were identified, and genes with the highest metagene scores were assigned to the corresponding module.
For traveling ratio, transcription efficiency, and read through index calculation, ChIP-seq densities of proximal promoter, gene body, and termination region were first summarized for each RNAPII mutant with DeepTools (v.3.3.1) using bigwigCompare function according to GENCODE annotation (v45). Then, traveling ratio, transcription efficiency, and read through index were calculated with proximal promoter dividing gene body, termination region dividing proximal promoter, and termination region dividing gene body for each gene, respectively. Limma (v.3.40.6) package was then used for differential analysis, following the manufacturer’s instruction. A cutoff of fold change> 1.5 and FDR < 0.01 was used to identify significant changed genes.
For CLK1, CLK4, and YES1 binding genes identification, MACS2 (v.2.2.7.1) was used to call peaks with cutoff of
q
value < 0.05 for two biological replicates, respectively. Then, the overlapped peaks of two replicates were obtained using bedtools intersect function with minimal overlap of 50% for each peak. Then, peaks were annotated with ChIPseeker (v.1.5.1) to their nearest genes. Then, the fragments per kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads (FPKM) of each peak was calculated, and genes with top 500 peaks were identified as the binding genes.
TT-seq data analysis
TT-seq analyses followed a similar approach to polyadenylate [poly(A)] RNA-seq with some modifications. Trimmed reads were mapped to the concatenated hg38-dm6 genome index with STAR (v.2.7.3a). Replicate BAM files were merged with the samtools merge function, and the merged BAM files were converted into BigWig files using the bamCoverage function. The TPM of RPB1 gene in RNAPII WT replacement cell and
D. melanogaster
(dm6) reads were used together to calculate spike-in normalization factor. To differentiate between sense and antisense strands, the bamCoverage function was applied with the “-filterRNAstrand” parameter set to forward or reverse. The visualization of genome-wide distributions was performed using DeepTools (v.3.3.1). The computeMatrix function was used to calculate read distribution across target regions, and the plotHeatmap function was used to generate meta-gene plots. To quantify gene expression, multibigwigsummary was used to summarize TT-seq signals on active genes, lncRNAs and snRNAs, respectively. Two-sided Wilcoxon tests were used to calculate significances between untreated and RNAPII
mut
groups. RNAPII
mut
TT-seq signaling dividing ChIP-seq was used to generate RNAPII velocity as described previously (
98
).

Quantitative ChIP-MS data analysis
Statistical analyses of proteomic data were conducted using the DEqMS R package (v.1.2.0), following the manufacturer’s guidelines. Missing values were imputed with MinProb function from MSnbase package (v.2.10.1). Also, data were normalized with library size. For endogenous RNAPII antibody ChIP-MS, IgG group is used as control group, and a cutoff of FDR < 0.05 and log
2

For cell proliferation assay, FACS, RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, CUT&Tag, TT-seq, and ChIP-MS, at least two biological replicates were performed.
